edition.alertText: IRGC declares Hormuz 'closed' — warns ships risk being 'engulfed in flames'; Brent eases to $114.51 (-1.89%) on Qatar mediation hopes; UKMTO reports vessel on fire near Al-Faw and tanker disabled; Houthis attack Riyadh airport hours after reopening; Egypt approves troop deployment to Saudi Arabia; Pezeshkian heads to Moscow; Israel votes today

situation: The Strait of Hormuz crisis entered day 241 with the IRGC taking the dramatic step of formally declaring the strait 'closed' on October 26, warning via Tasnim News Agency that violating vessels 'risk being engulfed in flames.' The declaration followed the deadliest month of the conflict — Lloyd's List Intelligence recorded at least 28 attacks or security incidents in and around the strait in October, more than double the monthly average since the war began. UKMTO issued two new warnings on October 26: a time-late report confirming an outbound tanker was struck and disabled by an unknown projectile at 0839 UTC on October 23 (crew safe), and a separate alert for a vessel on fire 63 nautical miles southeast of Al-Faw, Iraq, where a NASA satellite detected heat at 0926 hours. Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) non-compliant blacklist has grown to 123 vessels — up from 46 at its August 24 launch — with two new additions over the weekend including the Liberian-flagged VLCC Senegal Prosperity (Seatrade Maritime). Daily transits have collapsed to just 4 per day from a pre-war baseline of 85 (IMF PortWatch), while approximately 500 vessels remain delayed outside the strait. CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper flew over the strait on October 25, saying US forces had cleared primary shipping lanes of Iranian sea mines and maintained a 95% transit success rate, with over 3,000 commercial vessels facilitated and more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude exported since summer. Kpler's latest assessment reports cumulative Middle East crude and condensate production outages have passed 2 billion barrels, with 5 million b/d still offline — though total Middle East crude exports have temporarily returned to pre-war levels thanks to Saudi Arabia ramping East-West Pipeline flows to 5.8 million b/d.

Oil markets retreated on Monday as Qatari-mediated diplomacy raised fleeting hopes of de-escalation. Brent crude fell 1.89% to $114.51 per barrel — pulling back from its $116.72 Friday settlement, the highest since April — while WTI dropped 2.16% to $101.04 per barrel. Vandana Hari of Vanda Insights cautioned the reprieve 'may prove temporary.' The prior week's 6% Brent rally was fueled by Iran's 7-tanker attack claims on October 22, the supertanker mine strikes on October 24, and Houthi escalation against Saudi targets. Gold eased to around $4,002 per ounce after safe-haven flows had pushed it above $4,100 earlier in the week. VLCC tanker rates remained near record levels at $1.2–1.4 million per day for Gulf-to-East Asia routes, with freight adding $33–41 per barrel to delivered crude cost — more than a quarter of the delivered price. Newcastle coal held near $150 per tonne, up 40% year-to-date as the Hormuz gas shock continues to revive coal demand (Kalkine). Gulf stock markets fell in sympathy, with Saudi Arabia's benchmark index down 1.1% and Aramco shares declining 1.2%. US gasoline averaged $4.29 per gallon nationally with diesel at $6.35 — the highest since the 2022 spike. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve remains at its lowest level since 1982.

The Yemen theater escalated sharply alongside diplomatic maneuvers on multiple fronts. Houthi forces launched a missile barrage at Saudi Arabia on October 26, targeting Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport just hours after it partially reopened from a two-week closure following a deadly October attack that killed 13 and wounded over 300. The Saudi-led coalition intercepted at least 10 ballistic missiles aimed at the southern region, plus a cruise missile targeting Khamis Mushait, a ballistic missile and two drones aimed at Riyadh, and two missiles near the Makkah and Madina regions — with falling debris injuring two in the south. The coalition retaliated by destroying four Houthi missile launchers and five tunnel-stored missile depots in Sanaa. Egypt's parliament approved President Sisi's request to deploy troops to defend Saudi Arabia, described as defensive and not directed at Yemen. On the diplomatic front, Iran's President Pezeshkian traveled to Moscow for meetings with Putin and Qatar's Emir Tamim, while Qatari mediators continued shuttling proposals between Tehran and Washington. Saudi, Turkish, and Pakistani delegations met Iranian leaders in Tehran on Monday, with Iran's security chief Rezaei calling the talks 'very good' — though no concrete outcomes were announced. Trump said he was still deciding between a deal and action: 'Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal?' Meanwhile, Israel holds its general election on October 27, with Netanyahu and former army chief Eisenkot in a tight race that could reshape the war's trajectory.

supplyChain.name: Sulfur
supplyChain.text: Global exports down 39% YoY to 6.1M tonnes in Q2 (S&P). Sulfur prices above $1,000/tonne feeding into phosphate production costs — Egypt, Brazil, India cutting output. Mosaic idling South Fort Meade phosphate plant (Florida) for 6+ months from Dec 8 due to sulfur shortage. Morocco's OCP needs 3.7M tonnes/yr from the region. Nearly half of seaborne sulfur passed through Hormuz pre-war.

supplyChain.name: Sulfuric Acid
supplyChain.text: China banned exports Apr-Aug (700kt/yr quota replaced). SX-EW copper producers (15% of global cathode) fully exposed. Huayou cut Indonesian nickel HPAL output 50%.

supplyChain.name: Fertilizer
supplyChain.text: Fertilizer shipments through Hormuz 'close to zero' since early September; urea exports from Hormuz-dependent economies fell 83% YoY in April (ITC). ~850kt urea stranded. 4 of 5 Bangladesh urea plants shut since March due to LNG shortages. FAO Food Price Index at 136 (highest since Nov 2022). UNCTAD's de la Mora warns at Doha forum (Oct 25) that farmers cutting fertilizer use will affect 2027 crops; African nations Zimbabwe, Uganda face critical fuel/fertilizer shortfalls.

supplyChain.name: LNG
supplyChain.text: Qatar LNG exports still crippled — QatarEnergy signed historic deal to buy 4M tonnes/yr US LNG from Cheniere through 2054. Dutch TTF gas near €90/MWh. Japan's trade deficit doubled to ¥2.82T ($17.8B) on higher energy costs. Forbes warns next risk for US LNG is demand, not supply, as price dislocations persist. Kpler: Asian LNG prices to rise amid simmering geopolitical tensions and elevated TTF.

supplyChain.name: Petrochemicals
supplyChain.text: MEG ethylene/polyethylene exports disrupted. Gulf petrochem complex cut to ~60% capacity. Methanol down 80% (ITC). Dow, LyondellBasell margins widening on supply constraint.
